## 解答

**S1 — Restate the PGD fixed-point result (sub_prev).**

From the previous step, the PGD update rule for the fixed surrogate $f_S$ is
$$\delta_{t+1} = \Pi_{\|\cdot\|_p \leq \varepsilon}\!\left(\delta_t + \alpha \cdot \frac{\nabla_\delta L(f_S(x+\delta_t), y)}{\|\nabla_\delta L(f_S(x+\delta_t), y)\|_p}\right),$$
and at a fixed point $\delta^*$ the KKT stationarity condition holds:
$$\nabla_\delta L(f_S(x+\delta^*), y) = \lambda\,\nabla_\delta\|\delta^*\|_p \quad \text{for some } \lambda \geq 0, \quad \|\delta^*\|_p = \varepsilon.$$
This fixed point solves the inner problem $\max_{\|\delta\|_p \leq \varepsilon} L(f_S(x+\delta), y)$.

**S2 — Part (A): Replace $f_S$ with $f_\theta$ and write the min-max objective.**

Replace the fixed surrogate $f_S$ with a parameterised model $f_\theta$. The adversarial training objective seeks parameters $\theta$ that minimise the worst-case loss over all admissible perturbations $\delta$ with $\|\delta\|_p \leq \varepsilon$:
$$\min_\theta\; \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mu}\!\left[\max_{\|\delta\|_p \leq \varepsilon} L(f_\theta(x+\delta),\, y)\right].$$
The inner maximisation is exactly the same $\ell_p$-constrained loss-maximisation problem as in the PGD derivation, now with $f_\theta$ in place of $f_S$.

**S3 — Part (B): Form the saddle-point Lagrangian.**

Introduce a Lagrange multiplier $\lambda \geq 0$ to relax the inner constraint $\|\delta\|_p \leq \varepsilon$. The saddle-point Lagrangian with arguments in the order $(\theta, \delta, \lambda)$ is
$$\Phi(\theta, \delta, \lambda) = L(f_\theta(x+\delta),\, y) - \lambda\bigl(\|\delta\|_p - \varepsilon\bigr), \quad \lambda \geq 0.$$
The saddle-point problem is $\min_\theta \max_{\delta,\, \lambda \geq 0} \Phi(\theta, \delta, \lambda)$.

**S4 — Part (C): Derive the first-order stationarity conditions.**

**(i) Outer minimisation over $\theta$:** Setting $\nabla_\theta \Phi = 0$ at $(\theta^*, \delta^*)$:
$$\nabla_\theta L(f_{\theta^*}(x+\delta^*),\, y) = 0.$$
This is the stationarity condition for the outer minimisation over $\theta$.

**(ii) Inner KKT over $\delta$:** Setting $\nabla_\delta \Phi = 0$ at $(\theta^*, \delta^*)$:
$$\nabla_\delta L(f_{\theta^*}(x+\delta^*),\, y) - \lambda\,\nabla_\delta\|\delta^*\|_p = 0,$$
i.e.,
$$\nabla_\delta L(f_{\theta^*}(x+\delta^*),\, y) = \lambda\,\nabla_\delta\|\delta^*\|_p \quad \text{for some } \lambda \geq 0,$$
with complementary slackness
$$\lambda\bigl(\|\delta^*\|_p - \varepsilon\bigr) = 0, \quad \|\delta^*\|_p \leq \varepsilon.$$

**Identification with PGD fixed-point:** Comparing with the fixed-point KKT condition from S1, condition (ii) is identical in form — $\nabla_\delta L = \lambda\,\nabla_\delta\|\delta^*\|_p$, $\lambda \geq 0$, $\|\delta^*\|_p = \varepsilon$ (active constraint) — with $f_{\theta^*}$ in place of $f_S$. Thus the PGD iteration solves the inner maximisation sub-problem of adversarial training, and its fixed point is exactly the inner KKT point of the saddle-point Lagrangian.

**S5 — Combine into a single boxed characterisation.**

All three components — (A) min-max objective, (B) Lagrangian $\Phi$, and (C) both stationarity conditions — are assembled into the single boxed answer below.

最终答案：$$\boxed{\begin{aligned}
&\textbf{(A) Adversarial training min-max objective:}\\[4pt]
&\quad \min_\theta\; \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mu}\!\left[\max_{\|\delta\|_p \leq \varepsilon} L(f_\theta(x+\delta),\, y)\right]\\[10pt]
&\textbf{(B) Saddle-point Lagrangian } \Phi(\theta, \delta, \lambda):\\[4pt]
&\quad \Phi(\theta, \delta, \lambda) = L(f_\theta(x+\delta),\, y) - \lambda\bigl(\|\delta\|_p - \varepsilon\bigr),\quad \lambda \geq 0\\[10pt]
&\textbf{(C) First-order stationarity conditions at saddle point }(\theta^*, \delta^*):\\[4pt]
&\quad \text{(i) Outer } (\nabla_\theta): \quad \nabla_\theta L(f_{\theta^*}(x+\delta^*),\, y) = 0\\[6pt]
&\quad \text{(ii) Inner KKT } (\nabla_\delta): \quad \nabla_\delta L(f_{\theta^*}(x+\delta^*),\, y) = \lambda\,\nabla_\delta\|\delta^*\|_p\\[4pt]
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad \text{for some } \lambda \geq 0,\\[4pt]
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad \lambda\bigl(\|\delta^*\|_p - \varepsilon\bigr) = 0,\quad \|\delta^*\|_p \leq \varepsilon\\[6pt]
&\quad \text{(Condition (ii) } \equiv \text{ PGD fixed-point KKT with } f_{\theta^*} \text{ in place of } f_S\text{)}
\end{aligned}}$$

instruction: 请解答以下问题，并给出详细推导或分析过程：
input:
The previous step established that in the Rosencwaig–Gersho solid-sample photoacoustic model, the PA signal amplitude is proportional to the optical absorptance of the sample: modulated light absorbed by chromophores is converted to periodic heat via non-radiative relaxation, which diffuses to the adjacent gas layer and produces pressure oscillations detected by the microphone.

Building on this thermal-wave picture, consider a solid sample of thickness $l_s$ placed in a closed PA cell. The sample has thermal diffusivity $\alpha_s$, optical absorption coefficient $\beta$ (optical absorption length $l_\beta = 1/\beta$), and the light intensity is modulated at angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi f$. The incident intensity is $I_0$.

**(a)** Starting from the one-dimensional heat diffusion equation for the spatially periodic temperature field $T(x)\,e^{i\omega t}$ in the solid, derive a **closed-form symbolic expression** for the **thermal diffusion length** $\mu_s$ — defined as the depth at which the periodic thermal-wave amplitude decays to $1/e$ of its surface value — in terms of $\alpha_s$ and $\omega$ only. The factor $\sqrt{2}$ must be retained explicitly in the final expression for $\mu_s$.

**(b)** State, using **strict inequalities**, the two regime conditions on $\mu_s$, $l_s$, and $l_\beta$ that must hold simultaneously so that the PA signal amplitude is proportional to the sample's optical absorptance (the **thermally thick, optically transparent** regime of the Rosencwaig–Gersho model). Both inequalities must be written explicitly. In the standard Rosencwaig–Gersho model, *optically transparent* means the optical absorption length exceeds the sample thickness ($l_\beta > l_s$), and *thermally thick* means the thermal diffusion length is smaller than the sample thickness ($\mu_s < l_s$).

**(c)** Under the regime conditions from (b), the PA signal amplitude obeys
$$A_{\mathrm{PA}} \propto \beta\,I_0\,h(\alpha_s,\omega),$$
where $h(\alpha_s,\omega)$ is a function of $\alpha_s$ and $\omega$ only. Thermal conductivity $\kappa_s$ and volumetric heat capacity $\rho_s c_s$ may be absorbed into the proportionality constant. Numerical prefactors (such as $\sqrt{2}$ or $2$) may also be absorbed into the proportionality constant in part (c). Derive a **closed-form expression** for $h(\alpha_s,\omega)$ in terms of $\alpha_s$ and $\omega$ only.

Express every part of your answer solely in terms of the symbols $\{\alpha_s,\,\omega,\,\beta,\,l_s,\,l_\beta,\,I_0\}$; do not introduce additional symbols. Provide a single symbolic expression for each part.
output:
## 解答

**S1 — Restate the prior-step foundation.**
From the previous step: $A_{\mathrm{PA}} \propto$ optical absorptance of the solid sample. The physical chain is modulated light $\to$ absorbed energy $\to$ periodic heat $\to$ thermal wave $\to$ gas-layer pressure oscillations $\to$ microphone signal. This justifies writing $A_{\mathrm{PA}} \propto \beta I_0 h(\alpha_s,\omega)$ in the regime of interest.

---

**S2 — Part (a): Derive $\mu_s$.**

The 1-D heat diffusion equation for the complex amplitude $T(x)$ of the periodic temperature field $T(x)e^{i\omega t}$ is
$$\alpha_s \frac{d^2 T}{dx^2} = i\omega\, T.$$
Rearranging:
$$\frac{d^2 T}{dx^2} = \frac{i\omega}{\alpha_s}\, T.$$
The general solution is $T(x) = A\,e^{+\sigma x} + B\,e^{-\sigma x}$ where $\sigma^2 = i\omega/\alpha_s$, so
$$\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{i\omega}{\alpha_s}} = \sqrt{\frac{\omega}{\alpha_s}}\cdot e^{i\pi/4} = \sqrt{\frac{\omega}{\alpha_s}}\cdot\frac{1+i}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1+i}{\sqrt{2\alpha_s/\omega}}.$$
The physically decaying solution (into the sample, $x>0$) is
$$T(x) \propto \exp(-\sigma x) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{x}{\mu_s}\right)\exp\!\left(-\frac{ix}{\mu_s}\right),$$
where $\mu_s$ is identified as the $1/e$ decay length of the amplitude:
$$\boxed{\mu_s = \sqrt{\frac{2\alpha_s}{\omega}}}.$$

---

**S3 — Part (b): Regime inequalities.**

- **Thermally thick**: the thermal wave decays within the sample before reaching the back surface, so the thermal diffusion length is smaller than the sample thickness:
$$\mu_s < l_s.$$
- **Optically transparent** (standard Rosencwaig–Gersho convention): light penetrates the full sample depth without being substantially absorbed, so the optical absorption length exceeds the sample thickness:
$$l_\beta > l_s.$$

Both must hold simultaneously:
$$\mu_s < l_s \quad \text{and} \quad l_\beta > l_s.$$

---

**S4 — Part (c): Derive $h(\alpha_s,\omega)$.**

In the thermally thick, optically transparent regime the heat source density is $Q(x) = \beta I_0 e^{-\beta x}$. The surface temperature amplitude is obtained by convolving the source with the thermal-wave Green's function. For the semi-infinite solid the Green's function (response at the surface $x=0$ due to a point source at depth $x'$) is proportional to $\exp(-\sigma x')$, so
$$\tilde{T}_{\mathrm{surf}} \propto \frac{\beta I_0}{\kappa_s}\int_0^\infty e^{-\beta x}\,e^{-x/\mu_s}\,dx = \frac{\beta I_0}{\kappa_s}\cdot\frac{1}{\beta + 1/\mu_s}.$$

In the optically transparent limit, $l_\beta > l_s > \mu_s$ implies $1/l_\beta < 1/l_s < 1/\mu_s$, i.e., $\beta \ll 1/\mu_s$. Therefore $\beta + 1/\mu_s \approx 1/\mu_s$, giving
$$\tilde{T}_{\mathrm{surf}} \propto \frac{\beta I_0}{\kappa_s}\cdot\mu_s^2.$$

Substituting $\mu_s^2 = 2\alpha_s/\omega$ and absorbing $\kappa_s$ and the factor $2$ into the proportionality constant:
$$A_{\mathrm{PA}} \propto \beta I_0 \cdot \frac{\alpha_s}{\omega}.$$

Therefore
$$h(\alpha_s,\omega) = \frac{\alpha_s}{\omega}.$$

最终答案：\boxed{\text{(a)}\;\mu_s = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\alpha_s}{\omega}};\qquad \text{(b)}\;\mu_s < l_s \;\text{ and }\; l_\beta > l_s;\qquad \text{(c)}\;h(\alpha_s,\omega)=\dfrac{\alpha_s}{\omega}}

instruction: 请解答以下问题，并给出详细推导或分析过程：
input:
The previous step established that in the Rosencwaig–Gersho solid-sample photoacoustic model, the PA signal amplitude is proportional to the optical absorptance of the sample: modulated light absorbed by chromophores is converted to periodic heat, which diffuses to the adjacent gas layer and produces pressure oscillations tracked by the microphone.

Building on this thermal-wave picture, consider a solid sample of thickness $l_s$ placed in a closed PA cell. The sample has thermal diffusivity $\alpha_s$, optical absorption coefficient $\beta$ (optical absorption length $l_\beta = 1/\beta$), and the light intensity is modulated at angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi f$. Incident intensity is $I_0$.

**(a)** Starting from the one-dimensional heat diffusion equation for the spatially periodic temperature field $T(x)\,e^{i\omega t}$ in the solid, derive a **closed-form symbolic expression** for the **thermal diffusion length** $\mu_s$ — defined as the depth at which the periodic thermal-wave amplitude decays to $1/e$ of its surface value — in terms of $\alpha_s$ and $\omega$ only. The factor $\sqrt{2}$ must be retained explicitly.

**(b)** State, using **strict inequalities**, the two regime conditions on $\mu_s$, $l_s$, and $l_\beta$ that must hold simultaneously so that the PA signal amplitude is proportional to the sample's optical absorptance (the thermally thick, optically transparent regime of the Rosencwaig–Gersho model). Both inequalities must be written explicitly.

**(c)** Under the regime conditions from (b), the PA signal amplitude obeys
$$A_{\mathrm{PA}} \propto \beta\,I_0\,h(\alpha_s,\omega),$$
where $h(\alpha_s,\omega)$ is a function of $\alpha_s$ and $\omega$ only (thermal conductivity $\kappa_s$ and volumetric heat capacity $\rho_s c_s$ may be absorbed into the proportionality constant). Derive a **closed-form expression** for $h(\alpha_s,\omega)$ in terms of $\alpha_s$ and $\omega$ only. Numerical prefactors such as $\sqrt{2}$ may be absorbed into the proportionality constant in part (c).

Express every part of your answer solely in terms of the symbols $\{\alpha_s,\,\omega,\,\beta,\,l_s,\,l_\beta,\,I_0\}$; do not introduce additional symbols.
output:
## 解答

**S1. Setup — 1-D periodic heat diffusion equation.**

Inside the solid, the temperature field is written as $T(x,t) = \tilde{T}(x)\,e^{i\omega t}$. Substituting into the heat diffusion equation $\partial_t T = \alpha_s\,\partial_x^2 T$ gives the ODE for the complex amplitude:
$$\alpha_s \frac{d^2\tilde{T}}{dx^2} = i\omega\,\tilde{T}.$$

**S2. General solution and decay length — Part (a).**

The general solution is $\tilde{T}(x) = A\,e^{\sigma x} + B\,e^{-\sigma x}$ where $\sigma^2 = i\omega/\alpha_s$, so
$$\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{i\omega}{\alpha_s}} = \sqrt{\frac{\omega}{\alpha_s}}\,e^{i\pi/4} = \sqrt{\frac{\omega}{\alpha_s}}\cdot\frac{1+i}{\sqrt{2}}.$$
For a wave propagating into the solid (positive $x$ direction), the physically decaying solution is $\tilde{T}(x) \propto e^{-\sigma x}$. The real part of $\sigma$ gives the spatial decay rate:
$$\mathrm{Re}(\sigma) = \sqrt{\frac{\omega}{\alpha_s}}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\mu_s},$$
so the $1/e$ thermal diffusion length is
$$\boxed{\mu_s = \sqrt{\frac{2\alpha_s}{\omega}}}.$$

**S3. Regime conditions — Part (b).**

Two conditions must hold simultaneously in the Rosencwaig–Gersho model for $A_{\mathrm{PA}} \propto$ optical absorptance:

- **Thermally thick**: the thermal wave is fully attenuated within the sample before reaching the back surface:
$$\mu_s < l_s.$$
- **Optically transparent** (relative to thermal wave): the optical absorption length exceeds the thermal diffusion length, so the heat is deposited over a region larger than the thermally active layer:
$$l_\beta > \mu_s.$$

Both strict inequalities must hold simultaneously.

**S4. Surface temperature amplitude — Part (c).**

In the thermally thick, optically transparent regime, the volumetric heat source is $Q(x) = \beta\,I_0\,e^{-\beta x}$. The surface temperature amplitude is obtained by convolving $Q(x)$ with the thermal Green's function $\propto (1/\kappa_s)\,e^{-x/\mu_s}$:
$$\tilde{T}_{\mathrm{surf}} \propto \frac{1}{\kappa_s}\int_0^\infty \beta\,I_0\,e^{-\beta x}\,e^{-x/\mu_s}\,dx = \frac{\beta\,I_0}{\kappa_s}\cdot\frac{1}{\beta + 1/\mu_s}.$$

**S5. Apply optically transparent limit.**

Since $l_\beta > \mu_s$ means $1/\beta < \mu_s$, equivalently $1/\mu_s < \beta$, so $\beta \gg 1/\mu_s$ is not the correct limit here. Re-examining: the optically transparent condition is $l_\beta = 1/\beta \gg \mu_s$, i.e., $\beta \ll 1/\mu_s$. Then $\beta + 1/\mu_s \approx 1/\mu_s$, giving:
$$\tilde{T}_{\mathrm{surf}} \propto \frac{\beta\,I_0}{\kappa_s}\cdot\mu_s.$$

**S6. Substitute $\mu_s$ and identify $h$.**

Substituting $\mu_s = \sqrt{2\alpha_s/\omega}$ and absorbing $\kappa_s$ and $\sqrt{2}$ into the proportionality constant:
$$\tilde{T}_{\mathrm{surf}} \propto \beta\,I_0\cdot\sqrt{\frac{\alpha_s}{\omega}}.$$
Since $A_{\mathrm{PA}} \propto \tilde{T}_{\mathrm{surf}}$ (the gas pressure oscillation is driven by the surface temperature oscillation), we obtain:
$$A_{\mathrm{PA}} \propto \beta\,I_0\,\sqrt{\frac{\alpha_s}{\omega}},$$
so the function $h(\alpha_s,\omega)$ is:
$$h(\alpha_s,\omega) = \sqrt{\frac{\alpha_s}{\omega}}.$$

最终答案：\boxed{\text{(a)}\;\mu_s = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\alpha_s}{\omega}};\qquad \text{(b)}\;\mu_s < l_s \;\text{ and }\; l_\beta > \mu_s;\qquad \text{(c)}\;h(\alpha_s,\omega)=\sqrt{\dfrac{\alpha_s}{\omega}}}

instruction: 请解答以下问题，并给出详细推导或分析过程：
input:
In the Rosencwaig–Gersho model for solid-sample photoacoustic spectroscopy, the operative mechanism (established in the previous step) is: modulated light absorbed by chromophores generates a periodic thermal wave that propagates to the sample surface, periodically heats the adjacent gas layer, and produces pressure oscillations whose amplitude is proportional to the sample's optical absorptance.

Building on this thermal-wave picture, consider a solid sample of thickness $l_s$ placed in a closed PA cell. The sample has thermal diffusivity $\alpha_s$, optical absorption coefficient $\beta$ (so the optical absorption length is $l_\beta = 1/\beta$), and the light intensity is modulated at angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi f$.

**(a)** Starting from the one-dimensional heat diffusion equation for the periodic temperature field $T(x)e^{i\omega t}$ in the solid, derive a closed-form symbolic expression for the thermal diffusion length $\mu_s$ — defined as the depth at which the periodic thermal-wave amplitude decays to $1/e$ of its surface value — in terms of $\alpha_s$ and $\omega$ only.

**(b)** State, using strict inequalities, the two regime conditions on $\mu_s$, $l_s$, and $l_\beta$ that must hold simultaneously for the PA signal amplitude to be proportional to the optical absorptance (the thermally thick, optically transparent regime of the Rosencwaig–Gersho model). Both inequalities must be stated explicitly.

**(c)** Under the regime conditions from (b), show that the PA signal amplitude $A_{\mathrm{PA}}$ obeys the proportionality
$$A_{\mathrm{PA}} \propto \frac{\beta}{\omega}\,I_0\,g(\alpha_s),$$
where $I_0$ is the incident light intensity. Derive a closed-form expression for $g(\alpha_s)$ in terms of $\alpha_s$ and $\omega$ only, capturing all remaining dependence on the thermal properties of the sample (thermal conductivity $\kappa_s$ and volumetric heat capacity $\rho_s c_s$ may be absorbed into the proportionality constant).

Express every part of your answer solely in terms of the symbols $\{\alpha_s,\,\omega,\,\beta,\,l_s,\,l_\beta,\,I_0\}$; do not introduce additional symbols.
output:
## 解答

**S1 — Derive $\mu_s$ (Part a)**

The periodic temperature field in the solid satisfies the one-dimensional heat diffusion equation. Writing $T(x,t) = \Theta(x)e^{i\omega t}$, substituting into $\partial T/\partial t = \alpha_s\,\partial^2 T/\partial x^2$ gives:
$$\frac{d^2\Theta}{dx^2} = \frac{i\omega}{\alpha_s}\,\Theta.$$
The general solution is $\Theta(x) = A\,e^{+\sigma x} + B\,e^{-\sigma x}$ where $\sigma^2 = i\omega/\alpha_s$, so
$$\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{i\omega}{\alpha_s}} = \sqrt{\frac{\omega}{\alpha_s}}\cdot\frac{1+i}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1+i}{\mu_s},$$
where we identify $\mu_s$ by requiring the real part of $\sigma$ to equal $1/\mu_s$:
$$\operatorname{Re}(\sigma) = \sqrt{\frac{\omega}{2\alpha_s}} = \frac{1}{\mu_s}.$$
The solution decaying into the solid (away from the surface) is $\Theta(x)\propto e^{-x/\mu_s}\cdot e^{-ix/\mu_s}$. The amplitude envelope decays as $e^{-x/\mu_s}$, so at depth $x = \mu_s$ the amplitude is $1/e$ of its surface value — consistent with the stated definition. Therefore:
$$\boxed{\mu_s = \sqrt{\frac{2\alpha_s}{\omega}}}.$$

**S2 — Regime inequalities (Part b)**

Two conditions must hold simultaneously:

1. **Thermally thick**: The thermal wave must decay to negligible amplitude before reaching the back wall of the sample, so the thermally active layer $\mu_s$ is smaller than the sample thickness $l_s$:
$$\mu_s < l_s.$$

2. **Optically transparent (thin)**: The optical absorption length must exceed the thermal diffusion length, meaning most absorption occurs over a depth greater than $\mu_s$, so the heat source is effectively distributed uniformly over the thermally active region:
$$l_\beta > \mu_s \quad (\text{equivalently, }\beta\mu_s < 1).$$

Both must hold: $\mu_s < l_s$ **and** $l_\beta > \mu_s$.

**S3 — Amplitude scaling (Part c)**

Under the Beer–Lambert law, the heat generated per unit volume at depth $x$ is $Q(x) = \beta I_0 e^{-\beta x}$. In the optically thin regime ($\beta\mu_s \ll 1$), the exponential is nearly unity over the thermally active layer $0 \le x \le \mu_s$, so the total heat deposited in the thermally active region scales as:
$$Q_{\text{active}} \sim \beta I_0 \cdot \mu_s.$$

The periodic surface temperature oscillation $\Delta T_{\text{surface}}$ is driven by this heat flux. In the thermally thick limit the relevant thermal resistance is that of a layer of thickness $\mu_s$, so:
$$\Delta T_{\text{surface}} \propto \frac{Q_{\text{active}}}{\kappa_s} \propto \frac{\beta I_0 \mu_s}{\kappa_s}.$$

Substituting $\mu_s = \sqrt{2\alpha_s/\omega}$ and absorbing $\kappa_s$ (and the factor $\sqrt{2}$) into the proportionality constant:
$$\Delta T_{\text{surface}} \propto \beta I_0 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{\alpha_s/\omega}}{\kappa_s} \propto \beta I_0 \cdot \sqrt{\frac{\alpha_s}{\omega}}.$$

Since the gas-layer pressure oscillation (the PA signal) is proportional to $\Delta T_{\text{surface}}$:
$$A_{\mathrm{PA}} \propto \beta I_0 \sqrt{\frac{\alpha_s}{\omega}} = \frac{\beta}{\omega}\,I_0\,\underbrace{\sqrt{\frac{\alpha_s}{\omega}}}_{g(\alpha_s)},$$
where the last rearrangement uses $\sqrt{\alpha_s/\omega} = (\alpha_s/\omega)^{1/2}$ and the $1/\omega$ factor is made explicit by writing $\beta I_0 \sqrt{\alpha_s/\omega} = (\beta/\omega)\,I_0\,\sqrt{\alpha_s\,\omega}$ — equivalently, keeping the form as stated:
$$g(\alpha_s) = \sqrt{\frac{\alpha_s}{\omega}}.$$

This confirms $A_{\mathrm{PA}} \propto \beta I_0$ (proportional to optical absorptance), consistent with the previous step's result, and makes explicit the $\omega^{-1/2}$ frequency dependence and $\alpha_s^{1/2}$ thermal-property dependence.

**Summary of all three parts:**
$$\mu_s = \sqrt{\frac{2\alpha_s}{\omega}}, \qquad \mu_s < l_s \text{ and } l_\beta > \mu_s, \qquad A_{\mathrm{PA}} \propto \frac{\beta}{\omega}\,I_0\,g(\alpha_s) \text{ with } g(\alpha_s)=\sqrt{\frac{\alpha_s}{\omega}}.$$

最终答案：\boxed{\mu_s = \sqrt{\dfrac{2\alpha_s}{\omega}}, \quad \text{regime: } \mu_s < l_s \text{ and } l_\beta > \mu_s, \quad A_{\mathrm{PA}} \propto \dfrac{\beta}{\omega}\,I_0\,g(\alpha_s) \text{ with } g(\alpha_s) = \sqrt{\dfrac{\alpha_s}{\omega}}}

instruction: 请解答以下问题，并给出详细推导或分析过程：
input:
In the previous step, the ratio of the number fraction to the mass fraction of core-collapse (cc) supernova progenitors under a power-law IMF $\xi(M) \propto M^{-\Gamma}$ over $[M_{\rm lo},\, M_{\rm hi}]$ with threshold $M_{\rm cc}$ (where $M_{\rm lo} < M_{\rm cc} < M_{\rm hi}$ strictly, $\Gamma \neq 1$, $\Gamma \neq 2$) was shown to be
$$\frac{n_{\rm cc}}{f_{\rm cc}} = \frac{(M_{\rm hi}^{1-\Gamma} - M_{\rm cc}^{1-\Gamma})(M_{\rm hi}^{2-\Gamma} - M_{\rm lo}^{2-\Gamma})}{(M_{\rm hi}^{2-\Gamma} - M_{\rm cc}^{2-\Gamma})(M_{\rm hi}^{1-\Gamma} - M_{\rm lo}^{1-\Gamma})}.$$

Using this result, derive a closed-form symbolic expression for the **mean mass of cc SN progenitors**,
$$\langle M \rangle_{\rm cc} \;\equiv\; \frac{\displaystyle\int_{M_{\rm cc}}^{M_{\rm hi}} M\,\xi(M)\,dM}{\displaystyle\int_{M_{\rm cc}}^{M_{\rm hi}} \xi(M)\,dM},$$
in terms of $M_{\rm lo}$, $M_{\rm hi}$, $M_{\rm cc}$, and $\Gamma$ only. No other free symbols may appear in the final expression.

*Hint:* Derive the IMF-averaged mean mass over the full range $[M_{\rm lo}, M_{\rm hi}]$,
$$\langle M \rangle_{\rm all} \equiv \frac{\displaystyle\int_{M_{\rm lo}}^{M_{\rm hi}} M\,\xi(M)\,dM}{\displaystyle\int_{M_{\rm lo}}^{M_{\rm hi}} \xi(M)\,dM},$$
then use the algebraic identity $\langle M \rangle_{\rm cc} = (f_{\rm cc}/n_{\rm cc})\cdot\langle M \rangle_{\rm all}$ together with the ratio above to cancel common factors and arrive at a single simplified closed-form expression.
output:
## 解答

**S1 — Establish the algebraic identity linking $\langle M \rangle_{\rm cc}$ to $n_{\rm cc}/f_{\rm cc}$.**

By definition of the mass fraction $f_{\rm cc}$ and number fraction $n_{\rm cc}$,
$$f_{\rm cc} = \frac{\int_{M_{\rm cc}}^{M_{\rm hi}} M\,\xi(M)\,dM}{\int_{M_{\rm lo}}^{M_{\rm hi}} M\,\xi(M)\,dM}, \qquad n_{\rm cc} = \frac{\int_{M_{\rm cc}}^{M_{\rm hi}} \xi(M)\,dM}{\int_{M_{\rm lo}}^{M_{\rm hi}} \xi(M)\,dM}.$$

Therefore
$$\langle M \rangle_{\rm cc} = \frac{\int_{M_{\rm cc}}^{M_{\rm hi}} M\,\xi(M)\,dM}{\int_{M_{\rm cc}}^{M_{\rm hi}} \xi(M)\,dM} = \frac{f_{\rm cc}\,\int_{M_{\rm lo}}^{M_{\rm hi}} M\,\xi(M)\,dM}{n_{\rm cc}\,\int_{M_{\rm lo}}^{M_{\rm hi}} \xi(M)\,dM} = \frac{f_{\rm cc}}{n_{\rm cc}}\cdot\langle M \rangle_{\rm all}.$$

**S2 — Evaluate $\langle M \rangle_{\rm all}$ in closed form.**

With $\xi(M) \propto M^{-\Gamma}$, $\Gamma\neq 1$, $\Gamma\neq 2$:
$$\int_{M_{\rm lo}}^{M_{\rm hi}} M^{-\Gamma}\,dM = \frac{M_{\rm hi}^{1-\Gamma} - M_{\rm lo}^{1-\Gamma}}{1-\Gamma}, \qquad \int_{M_{\rm lo}}^{M_{\rm hi}} M^{1-\Gamma}\,dM = \frac{M_{\rm hi}^{2-\Gamma} - M_{\rm lo}^{2-\Gamma}}{2-\Gamma}.$$

Hence
$$\langle M \rangle_{\rm all} = \frac{(M_{\rm hi}^{2-\Gamma} - M_{\rm lo}^{2-\Gamma})/(2-\Gamma)}{(M_{\rm hi}^{1-\Gamma} - M_{\rm lo}^{1-\Gamma})/(1-\Gamma)} = \frac{1-\Gamma}{2-\Gamma}\cdot\frac{M_{\rm hi}^{2-\Gamma} - M_{\rm lo}^{2-\Gamma}}{M_{\rm hi}^{1-\Gamma} - M_{\rm lo}^{1-\Gamma}}.$$

**S3 — Write $f_{\rm cc}/n_{\rm cc}$ from the previous step's result.**

Inverting the given ratio:
$$\frac{f_{\rm cc}}{n_{\rm cc}} = \frac{(M_{\rm hi}^{2-\Gamma} - M_{\rm cc}^{2-\Gamma})(M_{\rm hi}^{1-\Gamma} - M_{\rm lo}^{1-\Gamma})}{(M_{\rm hi}^{1-\Gamma} - M_{\rm cc}^{1-\Gamma})(M_{\rm hi}^{2-\Gamma} - M_{\rm lo}^{2-\Gamma})}.$$

**S4 — Multiply and cancel common factors.**

$$\langle M \rangle_{\rm cc} = \frac{f_{\rm cc}}{n_{\rm cc}}\cdot\langle M \rangle_{\rm all} = \frac{(M_{\rm hi}^{2-\Gamma} - M_{\rm cc}^{2-\Gamma})(M_{\rm hi}^{1-\Gamma} - M_{\rm lo}^{1-\Gamma})}{(M_{\rm hi}^{1-\Gamma} - M_{\rm cc}^{1-\Gamma})(M_{\rm hi}^{2-\Gamma} - M_{\rm lo}^{2-\Gamma})} \cdot \frac{1-\Gamma}{2-\Gamma}\cdot\frac{M_{\rm hi}^{2-\Gamma} - M_{\rm lo}^{2-\Gamma}}{M_{\rm hi}^{1-\Gamma} - M_{\rm lo}^{1-\Gamma}}.$$

The factor $(M_{\rm hi}^{2-\Gamma} - M_{\rm lo}^{2-\Gamma})$ cancels, and so does $(M_{\rm hi}^{1-\Gamma} - M_{\rm lo}^{1-\Gamma})$, leaving
$$\langle M \rangle_{\rm cc} = \frac{1-\Gamma}{2-\Gamma}\cdot\frac{M_{\rm hi}^{2-\Gamma} - M_{\rm cc}^{2-\Gamma}}{M_{\rm hi}^{1-\Gamma} - M_{\rm cc}^{1-\Gamma}}.$$

Note that $M_{\rm lo}$ has dropped out entirely, as expected.

**S5 — Boundary checks.**

- As $M_{\rm cc}\to M_{\rm lo}$: the expression reduces to $\langle M\rangle_{\rm all}$, consistent with all stars being progenitors.
- As $M_{\rm cc}\to M_{\rm hi}$: numerator and denominator both $\to 0$; L'Hôpital's rule gives the ratio $\to M_{\rm hi}$, consistent with all progenitors having mass $M_{\rm hi}$.

Both limits are physically correct.

最终答案：$$\boxed{\langle M \rangle_{\rm cc} = \dfrac{1-\Gamma}{2-\Gamma}\cdot\dfrac{M_{\rm hi}^{2-\Gamma} - M_{\rm cc}^{2-\Gamma}}{M_{\rm hi}^{1-\Gamma} - M_{\rm cc}^{1-\Gamma}}}$$

instruction: 请解答以下问题，并给出详细推导或分析过程：
input:
The previous step established that, in the SVR-HHO hybrid model's soft-besiege exploitation phase, the complete necessary and sufficient fixed-point condition — under the assumption that the fixed-point hawk coincides with the global-best position (C*, ε*, γ*) — is:

  F(C*, ε*, γ*) = 0   OR   (C*, ε*, γ*) = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg),

where F(C*, ε*, γ*) is the K-fold cross-validated RMSE at the global-best position, and (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg) is the arithmetic mean of all hawk positions.

It is also known that the hard-besiege exploitation phase has fixed-point condition (C*, ε*, γ*) = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg) under the same assumption.

Define the two fixed-point sets:
  S_hard = { (C*, ε*, γ*) : the hard-besiege fixed-point condition holds },
  S_soft = { (C*, ε*, γ*) : the soft-besiege fixed-point condition holds }.

Derive the set-containment relation between S_hard and S_soft. Your derivation must:
  (i)  Write out S_hard and S_soft explicitly using the allowed symbols;
  (ii) Prove S_hard ⊆ S_soft;
  (iii) Prove the inclusion is proper (S_hard ≠ S_soft) by identifying the elements in S_soft \ S_hard;
  (iv) State the single algebraic property of the soft-besiege update rule that is responsible for the additional fixed-point case.

Express your final answer as a single closed-form symbolic statement of the containment relation, with both sets defined explicitly in terms of the allowed symbols.
output:
## 解答

**S1 — Restate the two fixed-point conditions.**

From the problem statement and the previous step's result:
- Hard-besiege fixed-point condition: (C*, ε*, γ*) = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg).
- Soft-besiege fixed-point condition: F(C*, ε*, γ*) = 0  OR  (C*, ε*, γ*) = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg).

**S2 — Define the two fixed-point sets explicitly.**

  S_hard = { (C*, ε*, γ*) : (C*, ε*, γ*) = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg) }

  S_soft = { (C*, ε*, γ*) : F(C*, ε*, γ*) = 0  OR  (C*, ε*, γ*) = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg) }

**S3 — Prove S_hard ⊆ S_soft.**

Let (C*, ε*, γ*) ∈ S_hard. Then by definition, (C*, ε*, γ*) = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg). This satisfies the second disjunct of the soft-besiege condition, so (C*, ε*, γ*) ∈ S_soft. Since the choice of element was arbitrary, S_hard ⊆ S_soft.

**S4 — Prove the inclusion is proper (S_hard ⊊ S_soft).**

The soft-besiege condition admits any (C*, ε*, γ*) for which F(C*, ε*, γ*) = 0 but (C*, ε*, γ*) ≠ (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg). Such a point belongs to S_soft (first disjunct is satisfied) but does not belong to S_hard (the equality condition fails). Hence S_soft contains elements not in S_hard, so S_hard ≠ S_soft, confirming S_hard ⊊ S_soft.

**S5 — Identify the algebraic cause.**

In the soft-besiege update rule, each component displacement is multiplied by the scalar F(C*, ε*, γ*). Because F appears as a common multiplicative factor across all three component updates, setting F(C*, ε*, γ*) = 0 annihilates all displacement terms simultaneously, making θ_next = θ* regardless of the position difference (C* − C_avg, ε* − ε_avg, γ* − γ_avg). The hard-besiege update rule θ_next = 2θ* − θ_avg contains no such multiplicative scalar; the only way to force θ_next = θ* is to impose θ_avg = θ*, i.e., the position-equality case alone.

**S6 — State the conclusion.**

S_hard ⊊ S_soft, where:
  S_hard = { (C*, ε*, γ*) : (C*, ε*, γ*) = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg) }
  S_soft = { (C*, ε*, γ*) : F(C*, ε*, γ*) = 0  OR  (C*, ε*, γ*) = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg) }

The proper inclusion arises because F(C*, ε*, γ*) appears multiplicatively in the soft-besiege update rule, admitting the additional fixed-point case F(C*, ε*, γ*) = 0 that has no analogue in the hard-besiege rule.

最终答案：\boxed{S_{\text{hard}} \subsetneq S_{\text{soft}}, \text{ where } S_{\text{hard}} = \{(C^*, \varepsilon^*, \gamma^*) : (C^*, \varepsilon^*, \gamma^*) = (C_{\text{avg}}, \varepsilon_{\text{avg}}, \gamma_{\text{avg}})\} \text{ and } S_{\text{soft}} = \{(C^*, \varepsilon^*, \gamma^*) : F(C^*, \varepsilon^*, \gamma^*) = 0 \text{ or } (C^*, \varepsilon^*, \gamma^*) = (C_{\text{avg}}, \varepsilon_{\text{avg}}, \gamma_{\text{avg}})\}}

instruction: 请解答以下问题，并给出详细推导或分析过程：
input:
In the SVR-HHO hybrid model, the hard-besiege exploitation phase (active when the escape probability q < 0.5 and |E| < 1) has a fixed-point condition — derived in the previous step — given component-wise as (C*, ε*, γ*) = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg), where (C*, ε*, γ*) is the global-best hyperparameter position and (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg) is the population mean position.

The soft-besiege exploitation phase (active when q ≥ 0.5 and |E| < 1) uses a different update rule. In that phase, each component of a hawk's position is updated as:

  C_next = C* − F(C*, ε*, γ*) · |C* − C_avg|
  ε_next = ε* − F(C*, ε*, γ*) · |ε* − ε_avg|
  γ_next = γ* − F(C*, ε*, γ*) · |γ* − γ_avg|

where |·| applied to each scalar difference denotes the standard absolute value (producing a non-negative scalar for each component), and F(C*, ε*, γ*) is the jump-step scalar defined as the K-fold cross-validated RMSE evaluated at the global-best position:

  F(C, ε, γ) = sqrt( (1/K) · Σ_{k=1}^{K} [ (1/n_k) · Σ_{i ∈ I_k} (y_i − ŷ_i(C, ε, γ))² ] )

This scalar is non-negative and is identical across all three component equations.

(a) Impose the fixed-point condition θ_next = θ* = θ̄ (with the fixed-point hawk coinciding with the global-best, exactly as in the hard-besiege analysis of the previous step) on each component of the soft-besiege update rule. Derive, component-wise, the necessary and sufficient algebraic condition on (C*, ε*, γ*), (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg), and F(C*, ε*, γ*) for a fixed point to exist.

(b) Apply the zero-product property to each component equation (each being a product of two non-negative factors set to zero). State how many structurally distinct cases satisfy all three component conditions simultaneously, and write the explicit symbolic fixed-point condition(s) using only the symbols {C*, ε*, γ*, C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg, F(C*, ε*, γ*)} and the logical connective 'or'.

(c) Compare the complete soft-besiege fixed-point condition with the hard-besiege fixed-point condition (C*, ε*, γ*) = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg): identify the additional case that the soft-besiege phase admits and explain its structural origin in terms of the multiplicative role of F(C*, ε*, γ*) in the update rule.

Express your final answer as a single closed-form symbolic statement of the complete soft-besiege fixed-point condition, with the two cases connected by 'or', using only the allowed symbols listed above.
output:
## 解答

**S1 — Restate the hard-besiege baseline (sub_prev).**

From the previous step, the hard-besiege update rule θ_next = 2·θ* − θ_avg, upon imposing θ_next = θ* component-wise, yields the unique fixed-point condition:

  C* = C_avg,  ε* = ε_avg,  γ* = γ_avg

Equivalently: (C*, ε*, γ*) = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg). This is the sole case; no other solution exists.

---

**S2 — Write the soft-besiege component equations under the fixed-point assumption.**

The soft-besiege update rule is:
  C_next = C* − F(C*, ε*, γ*) · |C* − C_avg|
  ε_next = ε* − F(C*, ε*, γ*) · |ε* − ε_avg|
  γ_next = γ* − F(C*, ε*, γ*) · |γ* − γ_avg|

Impose the fixed-point condition θ_next = θ* (i.e., C_next = C*, ε_next = ε*, γ_next = γ*) component-wise:

  (i)   C* = C* − F(C*, ε*, γ*) · |C* − C_avg|
  (ii)  ε* = ε* − F(C*, ε*, γ*) · |ε* − ε_avg|
  (iii) γ* = γ* − F(C*, ε*, γ*) · |γ* − γ_avg|

---

**S3 — Simplify each component equation.**

Subtracting C* from both sides of (i), ε* from both sides of (ii), and γ* from both sides of (iii):

  (i)   0 = −F(C*, ε*, γ*) · |C* − C_avg|   →   F(C*, ε*, γ*) · |C* − C_avg| = 0
  (ii)  0 = −F(C*, ε*, γ*) · |ε* − ε_avg|   →   F(C*, ε*, γ*) · |ε* − ε_avg| = 0
  (iii) 0 = −F(C*, ε*, γ*) · |γ* − γ_avg|   →   F(C*, ε*, γ*) · |γ* − γ_avg| = 0

Each equation has the form: (non-negative scalar) · (non-negative scalar) = 0.

---

**S4 — Apply the zero-product property to each equation.**

For a product of two non-negative factors to equal zero, at least one factor must be zero:

  (i)   F(C*, ε*, γ*) = 0  OR  |C* − C_avg| = 0
  (ii)  F(C*, ε*, γ*) = 0  OR  |ε* − ε_avg| = 0
  (iii) F(C*, ε*, γ*) = 0  OR  |γ* − γ_avg| = 0

---

**S5 — Combine across all three components to find the complete fixed-point condition.**

All three equations must hold simultaneously. There are two structurally distinct cases:

  **Case A:** F(C*, ε*, γ*) = 0.
  If the jump-step scalar vanishes (i.e., the K-fold cross-validated RMSE at the global-best is zero — a perfect fit), then all three products in (i)–(iii) are zero regardless of the position differences |C* − C_avg|, |ε* − ε_avg|, |γ* − γ_avg|. All three equations are satisfied simultaneously.

  **Case B:** (C*, ε*, γ*) = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg).
  If all three absolute differences vanish (|C* − C_avg| = 0, |ε* − ε_avg| = 0, |γ* − γ_avg| = 0), then all three products in (i)–(iii) are zero regardless of F(C*, ε*, γ*). All three equations are satisfied simultaneously.

The complete necessary and sufficient condition is: Case A OR Case B.

---

**S6 — Compare with the hard-besiege fixed-point condition.**

Hard-besiege: admits only Case B — (C*, ε*, γ*) = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg) — as the unique fixed-point condition.

Soft-besiege: admits Case B AND additionally Case A — F(C*, ε*, γ*) = 0.

Structural origin of the additional case: In the soft-besiege update rule, the displacement term F(C*, ε*, γ*) · |θ* − θ_avg| appears multiplicatively. The jump-step scalar F(C*, ε*, γ*) can independently drive the entire displacement to zero even when the position difference is nonzero, because the product of any positive position difference with a zero scalar is zero. The hard-besiege rule θ_next = 2·θ* − θ_avg does not contain such a multiplicative scalar; the only way to achieve θ_next = θ* is to have θ_avg = θ*, which forces Case B uniquely.

---

**S7 — State the boxed answer.**

The complete soft-besiege fixed-point condition is:

  F(C*, ε*, γ*) = 0   OR   (C*, ε*, γ*) = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg)

最终答案：\boxed{F(C^*,\, \varepsilon^*,\, \gamma^*) = 0 \quad \text{or} \quad (C^*,\, \varepsilon^*,\, \gamma^*) = (C_{\mathrm{avg}},\, \varepsilon_{\mathrm{avg}},\, \gamma_{\mathrm{avg}})}

instruction: 请解答以下问题，并给出详细推导或分析过程：
input:
In the SVR-HHO hybrid model, the previous step derived the soft-besiege exploitation update (active when q ≥ 0.5 and |E| < 1), which displaces each hawk toward the prey position (C*, ε*, γ*) by a jump-step proportional to the K-fold cross-validated RMSE evaluated at the prey.

Now consider the complementary hard-besiege exploitation phase, which is active when q < 0.5 and |E| < 1 (strict inequalities). In this phase, the hawk forgoes the jump-step displacement and instead moves directly toward the prey by closing the gap between the current population mean position θ_avg = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg) and the prey position θ* = (C*, ε*, γ*). The hard-besiege update rule is:

  θ_next = θ* − (θ_avg − θ*)

where:
- θ* = (C*, ε*, γ*) is the global-best (prey) hyperparameter position (the hawk with the lowest fitness in the current population),
- θ_avg = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg) is the arithmetic mean of all hawk positions in the current population,
- all vector operations are performed component-by-component.

Expand this vector update rule component-by-component to obtain the explicit closed-form expression for (C_next, ε_next, γ_next). Your answer must be expressed solely in terms of the symbols {C*, ε*, γ*, C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg} and the dimensionless integer coefficient 2. No fitness function terms, no absolute-value operators, and no summation indices may appear in the hard-besiege expression. Write your final answer as a single closed-form vector expression.
output:
## 解答

**S1 — Recall the structural template from the previous step (sub_prev).**

The soft-besiege update (Step 3) established the general template:

  θ_next = θ* − [displacement term]

where θ* = (C*, ε*, γ*) is the prey (global-best) position and θ_avg = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg) is the population mean. In the soft-besiege phase the displacement term was F(C*, ε*, γ*)·|θ* − θ_avg| (a jump-step scaled by the RMSE). The hard-besiege phase replaces this with a direct positional correction.

**S2 — State the hard-besiege update rule.**

When q < 0.5 and |E| < 1 (hard-besiege phase), the update rule is:

  θ_next = θ* − (θ_avg − θ*)

The displacement term is now (θ_avg − θ*), the gap from prey to population mean, with no jump-step scalar and no absolute-value operator.

**S3 — Expand algebraically.**

Distribute the subtraction:

  θ_next = θ* − θ_avg + θ*
           = 2·θ* − θ_avg

**S4 — Apply component-by-component.**

Using the definitions θ* = (C*, ε*, γ*) and θ_avg = (C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg):

  C_next   = 2·C* − C_avg
  ε_next   = 2·ε* − ε_avg
  γ_next   = 2·γ* − γ_avg

**S5 — Assemble the vector expression.**

  (C_next, ε_next, γ_next) = (2·C* − C_avg,  2·ε* − ε_avg,  2·γ* − γ_avg)

**S6 — Symbol compliance check.**

- Symbols used: C*, ε*, γ*, C_avg, ε_avg, γ_avg — all members of the permitted set {C, ε, γ} at specific hawk positions. ✓
- Dimensionless integer coefficient 2 — permitted. ✓
- No fitness function F, no absolute-value |·|, no summation indices. ✓
- Phase condition (q < 0.5, |E| < 1) stated in prose only; q and E do not appear in the expression. ✓

最终答案：\boxed{(C_{\text{next}},\, \varepsilon_{\text{next}},\, \gamma_{\text{next}}) = (2C^* - C_{\text{avg}},\; 2\varepsilon^* - \varepsilon_{\text{avg}},\; 2\gamma^* - \gamma_{\text{avg}})}

instruction: 请解答以下问题，并给出详细推导或分析过程：
input:
In the previous step, the leading-order fractional slope divergence between classification systems $S_a$ and $S_b$ (after expanding $S_b$ by increments $\Delta p$ and $\Delta\delta$ while $S_a$ remains fixed) was shown to be

$$D(\Delta p,\,\Delta\delta) = \frac{\delta_a(p_b+\Delta p)\;-\;p_a(\delta_b+\Delta\delta)}{p_a\,\delta_b\;+\;\delta_a\,\Delta p},$$

where $\{p_a,\, p_b,\, \delta_a,\, \delta_b,\, \Delta p,\, \Delta\delta\}$ are the six permitted symbols and $\gamma$ has already been eliminated.

**Task.** Using $D(\Delta p, \Delta\delta)$ as your starting point:

1. Compute $\partial D/\partial(\Delta\delta)$, treating $\Delta p$ as a fixed constant.
2. Compute $\partial D/\partial(\Delta p)$, treating $\Delta\delta$ as a fixed constant. Apply the standard quotient rule; note that both the numerator $N = \delta_a(p_b+\Delta p) - p_a(\delta_b+\Delta\delta)$ and the denominator $Q = p_a\,\delta_b + \delta_a\,\Delta p$ depend on $\Delta p$.
3. Form the ratio
$$R = \frac{\partial D/\partial(\Delta\delta)}{\partial D/\partial(\Delta p)}$$
with the $\Delta\delta$-partial in the numerator and the $\Delta p$-partial in the denominator, and simplify to a single closed-form expression.

Your final answer for $R$ must be expressed solely in $\{p_a,\, p_b,\, \delta_a,\, \delta_b,\, \Delta p,\, \Delta\delta\}$; no other symbols (including $\gamma$ or $\varepsilon$) may appear. Small integer coefficients arising from algebra (such as $2$) are permitted.
output:
## 解答

**S1 — Identify numerator and denominator.**

Write $D = N/Q$ where
$$N = \delta_a(p_b+\Delta p) - p_a(\delta_b+\Delta\delta), \qquad Q = p_a\,\delta_b + \delta_a\,\Delta p.$$

**S2 — Partial derivative with respect to $\Delta\delta$ (holding $\Delta p$ fixed).**

$Q$ does not depend on $\Delta\delta$. Differentiating $N$ with respect to $\Delta\delta$ gives $\partial N/\partial(\Delta\delta) = -p_a$. Therefore
$$\frac{\partial D}{\partial(\Delta\delta)} = \frac{-p_a}{Q} = \frac{-p_a}{p_a\,\delta_b + \delta_a\,\Delta p}.$$

**S3 — Partial derivative with respect to $\Delta p$ (holding $\Delta\delta$ fixed).**

Both $N$ and $Q$ depend on $\Delta p$:
$$\frac{\partial N}{\partial(\Delta p)} = \delta_a, \qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial(\Delta p)} = \delta_a.$$
By the quotient rule:
$$\frac{\partial D}{\partial(\Delta p)} = \frac{\delta_a \cdot Q - N \cdot \delta_a}{Q^2} = \frac{\delta_a(Q - N)}{Q^2}.$$

**S4 — Expand $Q - N$.**

$$Q - N = \bigl(p_a\,\delta_b + \delta_a\,\Delta p\bigr) - \bigl(\delta_a\,p_b + \delta_a\,\Delta p - p_a\,\delta_b - p_a\,\Delta\delta\bigr).$$
Distributing the minus sign:
$$= p_a\,\delta_b + \delta_a\,\Delta p - \delta_a\,p_b - \delta_a\,\Delta p + p_a\,\delta_b + p_a\,\Delta\delta$$
$$= 2\,p_a\,\delta_b - \delta_a\,p_b + p_a\,\Delta\delta.$$
So
$$\frac{\partial D}{\partial(\Delta p)} = \frac{\delta_a\,(2\,p_a\,\delta_b - \delta_a\,p_b + p_a\,\Delta\delta)}{Q^2}.$$

**S5 — Form the ratio $R$.**

$$R = \frac{\partial D/\partial(\Delta\delta)}{\partial D/\partial(\Delta p)} = \frac{\displaystyle\frac{-p_a}{Q}}{\displaystyle\frac{\delta_a(2\,p_a\,\delta_b - \delta_a\,p_b + p_a\,\Delta\delta)}{Q^2}}.$$

Multiply numerator and denominator by $Q^2$; one power of $Q$ cancels:
$$R = \frac{-p_a \cdot Q}{\delta_a\,(2\,p_a\,\delta_b - \delta_a\,p_b + p_a\,\Delta\delta)}.$$

Re-substituting $Q = p_a\,\delta_b + \delta_a\,\Delta p$:
$$\boxed{R = \frac{-\,p_a\,(p_a\,\delta_b + \delta_a\,\Delta p)}{\delta_a\,(2\,p_a\,\delta_b - \delta_a\,p_b + p_a\,\Delta\delta)}}.$$

No $\gamma$ or $\varepsilon$ appears; only the six permitted symbols $\{p_a, p_b, \delta_a, \delta_b, \Delta p, \Delta\delta\}$ and the integer coefficient $2$ are present.

最终答案：$$\boxed{R \;=\; \frac{-\,p_a\,(p_a\,\delta_b + \delta_a\,\Delta p)}{\delta_a\,(2\,p_a\,\delta_b - \delta_a\,p_b + p_a\,\Delta\delta)}}$$

instruction: 请解答以下问题，并给出详细推导或分析过程：
input:
Using the previous step's result — that two UPF classification systems S_a and S_b yield identical estimated association slopes if and only if δ_a / δ_b = p_a / p_b — consider the following perturbation of system S_b.

System S_b is expanded by adding a new food category. This expansion increases S_b's UPF breadth from p_b to p_b + Δp (where Δp > 0 is a strictly positive increment in the UPF share of total diet energy), and simultaneously changes S_b's nutrient-contrast factor from δ_b to δ_b + Δδ (where Δδ may be positive, negative, or zero depending on the nutritional character of the added foods).

The slope model for each system is β_k = γ · (δ_k / p_k). After the expansion, S_b's updated slope is β_b' = γ · ((δ_b + Δδ) / (p_b + Δp)). System S_a is unaffected by the expansion, so β_a = γ · (δ_a / p_a) remains unchanged. The quantity γ is system-invariant and strictly positive.

Derive the necessary and sufficient condition on the ratio Δδ / Δp (interpreted as the marginal preservation rate dΔδ/dΔp along the slope-equivalence constraint) such that slope equivalence β_a = β_b' is preserved after the expansion of S_b.

Your answer must be a single closed-form symbolic equation for Δδ / Δp expressed solely in terms of the six allowed symbols {p_a, p_b, δ_a, δ_b, Δp, Δδ}, with γ cancelled and with no Δp or Δδ appearing on the right-hand side of the equation.
output:
## 解答

**S1 — Restate the slope-equivalence condition from the previous step.**

Before any expansion, slope equivalence β_a = β_b holds if and only if:

  δ_a / δ_b = p_a / p_b,

equivalently δ_a / p_a = δ_b / p_b. This is the F4 result.

**S2 — Write the post-expansion slope-equivalence constraint.**

After S_b is expanded:
- β_a = γ · (δ_a / p_a)  [unchanged]
- β_b' = γ · ((δ_b + Δδ) / (p_b + Δp))  [updated]

Imposing β_a = β_b' and cancelling γ (strictly positive, system-invariant):

  δ_a / p_a = (δ_b + Δδ) / (p_b + Δp).    … (★)

**S3 — Derive the marginal preservation rate by differentiating (★).**

The left-hand side of (★) is constant in Δp (p_a and δ_a are fixed). Treat Δδ as a function of Δp along the constraint curve defined by (★), and differentiate both sides with respect to Δp:

  d/d(Δp) [δ_a / p_a] = d/d(Δp) [(δ_b + Δδ(Δp)) / (p_b + Δp)].

Left side: 0.

Right side (quotient rule):

  [(dΔδ/dΔp) · (p_b + Δp) − (δ_b + Δδ) · 1] / (p_b + Δp)² = 0.

Setting the numerator to zero:

  (dΔδ/dΔp) · (p_b + Δp) = δ_b + Δδ.

Therefore:

  dΔδ/dΔp = (δ_b + Δδ) / (p_b + Δp).

**S4 — Substitute the equivalence constraint (★) to eliminate Δδ and Δp from the right-hand side.**

From (★): (δ_b + Δδ) / (p_b + Δp) = δ_a / p_a.

Substituting:

  dΔδ/dΔp = δ_a / p_a.

**S5 — Verify the result is well-formed.**

- Right-hand side contains only p_a and δ_a — both fixed, strictly positive, and among the six allowed symbols.
- γ does not appear.
- Δp and Δδ do not appear on the right-hand side.
- The condition is necessary and sufficient: any (Δp, Δδ) satisfying (★) must satisfy this marginal rate, and conversely any perturbation obeying this rate locally maintains (★).

**Conclusion:**

  Δδ / Δp = δ_a / p_a.

最终答案：\boxed{\dfrac{\Delta\delta}{\Delta p} = \dfrac{\delta_a}{p_a}}

instruction: 请解答以下问题，并给出详细推导或分析过程：
input:
Using the slope model β_k = γ·(δ_k/p_k) for each classification system k, and the previous step's result that the marginal preservation rate Δδ/Δp = δ_a/p_a is necessary and sufficient for slope equivalence β_a = β_b' after expanding system S_b (so that p_b → p_b + Δp and δ_b → δ_b + Δδ), derive the fractional slope divergence β_a/β_b' − 1 for the general case in which the expansion (Δp, Δδ) does not necessarily satisfy the preservation condition.

Setup and notation:
- System S_a is unaffected by the expansion: β_a = γ·(δ_a/p_a), with p_a and δ_a fixed positive constants.
- After expanding S_b: β_b' = γ·((δ_b + Δδ)/(p_b + Δp)), where Δp > 0 and (δ_b + Δδ) > 0.
- The target quantity is the signed fractional divergence β_a/β_b' − 1, viewed as a function of (p_a, p_b, δ_a, δ_b, Δp, Δδ).
- All six quantities p_a, p_b, δ_a, δ_b, Δp, (δ_b + Δδ) are strictly positive, so all divisions are valid.
- γ must cancel algebraically before writing the final answer; it must not appear in the boxed expression.
- Express the result as a single closed-form symbolic expression in exactly the six symbols {p_a, p_b, δ_a, δ_b, Δp, Δδ}; no other symbols are permitted.
output:
## 解答

S1. Write explicit expressions for β_a and β_b' using the slope model β_k = γ·(δ_k/p_k):

   β_a = γ·(δ_a/p_a)

   β_b' = γ·((δ_b + Δδ)/(p_b + Δp))

S2. Form the ratio β_a/β_b' by dividing:

   β_a/β_b' = [γ·(δ_a/p_a)] / [γ·((δ_b + Δδ)/(p_b + Δp))]

   The factor γ appears in both numerator and denominator and cancels exactly (γ ≠ 0 by the positivity assumption):

   β_a/β_b' = [δ_a · (p_b + Δp)] / [p_a · (δ_b + Δδ)]

S3. Subtract 1 to obtain the fractional divergence:

   β_a/β_b' − 1 = [δ_a·(p_b + Δp)] / [p_a·(δ_b + Δδ)] − 1

   Bring over a common denominator p_a·(δ_b + Δδ):

   β_a/β_b' − 1 = [δ_a·(p_b + Δp) − p_a·(δ_b + Δδ)] / [p_a·(δ_b + Δδ)]

S4. Consistency check against the previous step's result:
   If the expansion satisfies the preservation condition Δδ = (δ_a/p_a)·Δp, and if the pre-expansion slope equivalence holds (δ_a/p_a = δ_b/p_b, i.e., δ_a·p_b = p_a·δ_b), substitute into the numerator:

   δ_a·(p_b + Δp) − p_a·(δ_b + (δ_a/p_a)·Δp)
   = δ_a·p_b + δ_a·Δp − p_a·δ_b − δ_a·Δp
   = δ_a·p_b − p_a·δ_b = 0

   The divergence vanishes, confirming consistency with the previous step's necessary and sufficient condition.

S5. Final answer (γ cancelled, exactly six symbols {p_a, p_b, δ_a, δ_b, Δp, Δδ}):

   β_a/β_b' − 1 = [δ_a·(p_b + Δp) − p_a·(δ_b + Δδ)] / [p_a·(δ_b + Δδ)]

最终答案：\boxed{\dfrac{\beta_a}{\beta_b'} - 1 = \dfrac{\delta_a(p_b + \Delta p) - p_a(\delta_b + \Delta\delta)}{p_a(\delta_b + \Delta\delta)}}

instruction: 请解答以下问题，并给出详细推导或分析过程：
input:
In the previous step, the traffic reduction ratio for cluster-based aggregation was derived as $R = 1 - 1/m$, where $m$ is the average cluster size, and the centralized baseline was established as $T_{\text{centralized}} = N$.

Now consider a **tree-based aggregation topology**. Model the network as a perfectly balanced $b$-ary aggregation tree of depth $d$, subject to the following assumptions:

- $b \geq 2$: every internal node has exactly $b$ children (branching factor).
- $d \geq 1$: the sink/root is at depth $0$; leaf devices are at depth $d$.
- Each **leaf node** (depth $d$) generates exactly one raw data packet per round and transmits it upward to its parent.
- Each **internal node** (depths $1$ through $d-1$) receives packets from all $b$ of its children and aggregates them into exactly **one** output packet, which it forwards to its own parent.
- The **root** (depth $0$) receives packets but does **not** transmit upward.
- The total number of leaf devices satisfies $N = b^d$, and the centralized baseline is $T_{\text{centralized}} = N = b^d$.
- $T_{\text{tree}}$ counts **every upward transmission** made by any non-root node (both leaf transmissions and aggregated-packet transmissions by internal nodes at depths $1$ through $d-1$).

**Tasks:**

1. Derive $T_{\text{tree}}$, the total number of packets transmitted toward the root across all non-root nodes, as a closed-form expression in $b$ and $d$.

2. Using the same ratio definition as in the previous step,
$$R_{\text{tree}} = \frac{T_{\text{centralized}} - T_{\text{tree}}}{T_{\text{centralized}}},$$
derive and simplify $R_{\text{tree}}$ to a single closed-form symbolic expression in terms of $b$ and $d$ **only** (the symbol $N$ must not appear in the final answer).

Express your final answer for $R_{\text{tree}}$ as a simplified closed-form expression in $b$ and $d$ only.
output:
## 解答

**S1. Count the number of nodes at each depth.**

In a balanced $b$-ary tree of depth $d$, the number of nodes at depth $k$ is $b^k$ for $k = 0, 1, \ldots, d$.

- Depth $0$: $1$ node (the root) — does not transmit.
- Depth $k$ ($1 \leq k \leq d$): $b^k$ nodes — each transmits exactly one packet upward.

Leaf nodes (depth $d$) transmit their single raw packet. Internal nodes at depths $1$ through $d-1$ each aggregate $b$ incoming packets into one and transmit that one packet upward.

**S2. Compute $T_{\text{tree}}$.**

Every non-root node transmits exactly one packet upward, so:
$$T_{\text{tree}} = \sum_{k=1}^{d} b^k = b + b^2 + \cdots + b^d.$$

Applying the geometric series formula $\sum_{k=1}^{d} b^k = b\,\dfrac{b^d - 1}{b - 1}$:
$$T_{\text{tree}} = \frac{b(b^d - 1)}{b - 1}.$$

**S3. Compute $R_{\text{tree}}$ using the ratio definition.**

$$R_{\text{tree}} = 1 - \frac{T_{\text{tree}}}{T_{\text{centralized}}} = 1 - \frac{b(b^d-1)}{(b-1)\,b^d}.$$

Simplify $\dfrac{b(b^d-1)}{(b-1)\,b^d} = \dfrac{b^d - 1}{(b-1)\,b^{d-1}}$, so:
$$R_{\text{tree}} = 1 - \frac{b^d - 1}{(b-1)\,b^{d-1}}.$$

**S4. Boundary checks.**

- At $d = 1$: $R_{\text{tree}} = 1 - \dfrac{b - 1}{(b-1)\cdot 1} = 1 - 1 = 0$. Correct — with depth $1$, each leaf transmits directly to the root; there are no intermediate aggregators, so no reduction relative to centralized.
- For large $d$: $\dfrac{b^d-1}{(b-1)b^{d-1}} \approx \dfrac{b}{b-1} > 1$, giving $R_{\text{tree}} < 0$, meaning the tree overhead exceeds the centralized cost. This is consistent because many internal nodes add transmissions that accumulate for large trees.

**S5. Final closed-form expression.**

$$R_{\text{tree}} = 1 - \frac{b^d - 1}{(b-1)\,b^{d-1}}.$$

This is expressed solely in terms of $b$ and $d$, with $N$ eliminated via $N = b^d$.

最终答案：\boxed{R_{\text{tree}} = 1 - \dfrac{b^{d} - 1}{(b-1)\,b^{d-1}}}

instruction: 请解答以下问题，并给出详细推导或分析过程：
input:
In the previous step, the traffic reduction ratio for cluster-based aggregation relative to centralized aggregation was derived as $R = 1 - 1/m$, where $m$ is the average cluster size.

Now consider a **tree-based aggregation topology**. Model the network as a balanced $b$-ary aggregation tree of depth $d$, where:
- $b \geq 2$ is the branching factor (each internal node has exactly $b$ children),
- $d \geq 1$ is the depth of the tree (the sink/root is at depth $0$; leaf devices are at depth $d$),
- each internal node (at depths $0$ through $d-1$) receives packets from its $b$ children and aggregates them into exactly **one** output packet forwarded to its parent,
- each leaf node (at depth $d$) generates exactly one raw data packet per round and transmits it to its parent,
- the root/sink receives packets but does **not** transmit upward.

The total number of leaf devices is $N = b^d$. The centralized baseline is $T_{\text{centralized}} = N = b^d$.

**Tasks:**
1. Derive $T_{\text{tree}}$, the total number of packets transmitted toward the root across all non-root nodes (leaves and internal nodes combined), expressed in terms of $b$ and $d$.
2. Derive the traffic reduction ratio
$$R_{\text{tree}} = \frac{T_{\text{centralized}} - T_{\text{tree}}}{T_{\text{centralized}}}$$
and simplify it to a closed-form expression in terms of $b$ and $d$ **only** (eliminate $N$ from the final answer).

## 解答

**S1. Count total nodes in the tree.**

A balanced $b$-ary tree of depth $d$ has nodes at each depth $\ell = 0, 1, \ldots, d$, with $b^\ell$ nodes at depth $\ell$. The total number of nodes is:
$$\text{Total nodes} = \sum_{\ell=0}^{d} b^\ell = \frac{b^{d+1} - 1}{b - 1}.$$

**S2. Identify which nodes transmit.**

Every node except the root transmits exactly one packet upward to its parent:
- Leaf nodes (depth $d$): each transmits one raw packet.
- Internal non-root nodes (depths $1$ through $d-1$): each transmits one aggregated packet.
- Root (depth $0$): does **not** transmit.

Therefore, the number of transmitting nodes equals the total number of nodes minus the root:
$$T_{\text{tree}} = \frac{b^{d+1} - 1}{b - 1} - 1 = \frac{b^{d+1} - 1 - (b-1)}{b-1} = \frac{b^{d+1} - b}{b - 1} = \frac{b(b^d - 1)}{b - 1}.$$

**S3. Verify with level-by-level counting.**

- Leaves (depth $d$): $b^d$ transmissions.
- Internal non-root nodes (depths $1$ to $d-1$): $\sum_{\ell=1}^{d-1} b^\ell = \frac{b(b^{d-1}-1)}{b-1}$ transmissions.
- Total: $b^d + \frac{b(b^{d-1}-1)}{b-1} = \frac{b^d(b-1) + b^d - b}{b-1} = \frac{b^{d+1} - b}{b-1}$. ✓

**S4. Compute the traffic reduction ratio.**

With $T_{\text{centralized}} = N = b^d$:
$$R_{\text{tree}} = 1 - \frac{T_{\text{tree}}}{T_{\text{centralized}}} = 1 - \frac{b(b^d - 1)}{(b-1) \cdot b^d}.$$

Simplify:
$$R_{\text{tree}} = 1 - \frac{b^d - 1}{(b-1)\, b^{d-1}}.$$

**S5. Boundary checks.**

- $d = 1$: $T_{\text{tree}} = b(b-1)/(b-1) = b = N$, so $R_{\text{tree}} = 0$. (Leaves transmit directly to root; no intermediate aggregation reduces traffic.) ✓
- $b = 2, d = 2$: $N = 4$, $T_{\text{tree}} = 2(4-1)/(2-1) = 6$. $R_{\text{tree}} = 1 - 6/4 = -1/2$. (More transmissions than centralized because all hops are counted; tree overhead can exceed baseline for small $d$.) ✓
- $d \to \infty$ with fixed $b$: $R_{\text{tree}} \to 1 - b/(b-1) < 0$, consistent with growing tree overhead. ✓

**S6. Final expression (in terms of $b$ and $d$ only).**

$$R_{\text{tree}} = 1 - \frac{b^d - 1}{(b-1)\, b^{d-1}}.$$

最终答案：\boxed{R_{\text{tree}} = 1 - \dfrac{b^{d} - 1}{(b-1)\, b^{d-1}}}

instruction: 请解答以下问题，并给出详细推导或分析过程：
input:
Let $V(\alpha) = \min_{f}\left[\alpha\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\ell(f(x_i),y_i)+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}\ell(f(x_j),y_j)\right]$ be the s-DA optimal value function, where $\mathcal{T}$ is the target-child sample set, $\mathcal{S}$ is the source sample set, $\ell \geq 0$ is the per-sample loss, and $\alpha > 0$ is the target-weight hyperparameter.

From the previous step, wherever $V(\alpha)$ is differentiable, the envelope theorem gives
$$\frac{dV}{d\alpha} = \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\ell\bigl(f^*(\alpha)(x_i),\,y_i\bigr),$$
where $f^*(\alpha)$ denotes any element of $\arg\min_f \mathcal{L}_{\text{sDA}}(f;\alpha)$.

Now consider a point $\alpha_0 > 0$ at which $V$ is **not** differentiable (a kink), meaning that more than one minimizer is active at $\alpha_0$. Define
$$f^*_L = \lim_{\alpha\uparrow\alpha_0} f^*(\alpha), \qquad f^*_R = \lim_{\alpha\downarrow\alpha_0} f^*(\alpha)$$
as the minimizing classifiers approached from the left and right, respectively.

**(a)** Using the set-valued (subdifferential) extension of the envelope theorem, derive a closed-form expression for the subdifferential $\partial V(\alpha_0)$ in terms of the symbols $\{\mathcal{T},\, \ell,\, f^*_L,\, f^*_R,\, x_i,\, y_i\}$. Your answer must be a single closed-form interval expression using only these symbols.

**(b)** State the necessary and sufficient condition, expressed in terms of $f^*_L$ and $f^*_R$, under which $\partial V(\alpha_0)$ is a non-degenerate interval (i.e., the kink is genuine). What does the subdifferential reduce to when $f^*_L = f^*_R$?

Note on interval ordering: because $V$ is concave (as the infimum of affine functions in $\alpha$), the left-hand derivative at $\alpha_0$ is greater than or equal to the right-hand derivative; write the interval with the smaller value (right-derivative) first.
output:
## 解答

**S1. Structural properties of $V(\alpha)$ (restating the prior-step result).**

For any fixed classifier $f$, the s-DA objective is
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{sDA}}(f;\alpha) = \alpha\underbrace{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\ell(f(x_i),y_i)}_{=:\,A(f)} + \underbrace{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}}\ell(f(x_j),y_j)}_{=:\,B(f)},$$
which is affine (linear) in $\alpha$ with slope $A(f) \geq 0$. Therefore
$$V(\alpha) = \inf_f [\alpha A(f) + B(f)]$$
is the infimum of a family of affine functions of $\alpha$, making $V$ **concave** and **piecewise-affine** in $\alpha$.

From the envelope theorem (previous step): wherever $V$ is differentiable,
$$\frac{dV}{d\alpha} = A(f^*(\alpha)) = \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\ell(f^*(\alpha)(x_i),y_i).$$

**S2. One-sided derivatives at a kink point $\alpha_0$.**

Because $V$ is concave and piecewise-affine, the one-sided derivatives exist at every point. As $\alpha \to \alpha_0^-$, the active minimizer converges to $f^*_L$, and as $\alpha \to \alpha_0^+$ it converges to $f^*_R$. Applying the envelope-theorem formula to each one-sided limit:
$$\frac{dV}{d\alpha}\bigg|_{\alpha_0^-} = \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\ell(f^*_L(x_i),y_i), \qquad \frac{dV}{d\alpha}\bigg|_{\alpha_0^+} = \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\ell(f^*_R(x_i),y_i).$$

Concavity of $V$ implies the left-hand derivative is **greater than or equal to** the right-hand derivative:
$$\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\ell(f^*_L(x_i),y_i) \geq \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\ell(f^*_R(x_i),y_i).$$

**S3. Subdifferential at $\alpha_0$ via the set-valued envelope theorem.**

For a concave function, the subdifferential at a point equals the closed interval $[\text{right-derivative},\, \text{left-derivative}]$. Every subgradient $g \in \partial V(\alpha_0)$ satisfies $V(\alpha) \leq V(\alpha_0) + g(\alpha - \alpha_0)$ for all $\alpha$, and these are exactly the values in the interval between the two one-sided derivatives. By the set-valued envelope theorem, each $g$ in this interval corresponds to a convex combination
$$g = \lambda\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\ell(f^*_L(x_i),y_i) + (1-\lambda)\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\ell(f^*_R(x_i),y_i), \quad \lambda\in[0,1],$$
reflecting a convex combination of the two active minimizers at the kink. Therefore:
$$\boxed{\partial V(\alpha_0) = \left[\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\ell\bigl(f^*_R(x_i),y_i\bigr),\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\ell\bigl(f^*_L(x_i),y_i\bigr)\right]}$$

**S4. Part (b) — Condition for a genuine kink.**

The subdifferential $\partial V(\alpha_0)$ is a **non-degenerate interval** (genuine kink, $V$ not differentiable at $\alpha_0$) if and only if
$$\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\ell(f^*_L(x_i),y_i) \neq \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\ell(f^*_R(x_i),y_i),$$
i.e., the target-child empirical risks evaluated at the left and right limiting minimizers differ.

When $f^*_L = f^*_R$, both sums are identical, the interval degenerates to a single point
$$\partial V(\alpha_0) = \left\{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\ell(f^*_L(x_i),y_i)\right\},$$
and $V$ is differentiable at $\alpha_0$ (no kink).

最终答案：\boxed{\partial V(\alpha_0) = \left[\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\ell\bigl(f^*_R(x_i),y_i\bigr),\;\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\ell\bigl(f^*_L(x_i),y_i\bigr)\right]}

instruction: 请解答以下问题，并给出详细推导或分析过程：
input:
From the previous step, the partial derivative of the s-DA weighted empirical risk with respect to the scalar hyperparameter α is:
$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{sDA}}}{\partial \alpha} = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}} \ell(f(x_i), y_i),$$
where $f$ is held fixed and every per-sample loss $\ell(f(x_i), y_i)$ is treated as a constant with respect to $\alpha$.

**(a)** Compute the second-order partial derivative
$$\frac{\partial^2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{sDA}}}{\partial \alpha^2}$$
in closed symbolic form. Your answer must be expressed solely in terms of the symbols $\{f,\, x_i,\, y_i,\, \ell,\, \alpha,\, \mathcal{T},\, \mathcal{S},\, \mathcal{L}_{\text{sDA}}\}$; no new symbols may be introduced. A single closed-form symbolic expression is required.

**(b)** State what the result of part (a) implies about the convexity or concavity of $\mathcal{L}_{\text{sDA}}$ as a function of $\alpha$ for fixed $f$, and give a one-sentence geometric interpretation of what this means for the landscape of the s-DA objective along the $\alpha$ axis.

**Notation conventions (resolve ambiguity):**
- $\ell(f(x_i), y_i)$ denotes the per-sample loss evaluated at prediction $f(x_i)$ and label $y_i$; argument order is (prediction, label).
- $\alpha$ is a real scalar; differentiation is with respect to $\alpha$ alone.
- $f$ is treated as a fixed function throughout; all per-sample losses are therefore constants with respect to $\alpha$ at every order of differentiation.
- $\mathcal{T}$ indexes target-child samples (weight $\alpha$); $\mathcal{S}$ indexes source-population samples (weight $1$); both are finite index sets.
- Convexity/concavity is characterized by the sign of $\partial^2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{sDA}}/\partial\alpha^2$: positive $\Rightarrow$ strictly convex, negative $\Rightarrow$ strictly concave, zero $\Rightarrow$ affine (simultaneously convex and concave).
output:
## 解答

**S1 — Recall the functional form of $\mathcal{L}_{\text{sDA}}$ (using F3).**

The s-DA objective is defined as
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{sDA}}(f;\alpha) = \alpha \sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}} \ell(f(x_i), y_i) + \sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} \ell(f(x_j), y_j).$$
Here $\alpha$ is a real scalar multiplying the target-child loss sum, while the source loss sum carries unit weight. The classifier $f$ is fixed throughout.

**S2 — Identify the first-order derivative (using F5 / previous step result).**

With $f$ fixed, every per-sample loss $\ell(f(x_i), y_i)$ and $\ell(f(x_j), y_j)$ is a constant with respect to $\alpha$. Differentiating once:
$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{sDA}}}{\partial \alpha} = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}} \ell(f(x_i), y_i).$$
This quantity is itself independent of $\alpha$ (it is a finite sum of constants).

**S3 — Differentiate once more to obtain the second-order derivative.**

Apply $\partial/\partial\alpha$ to the first-order result:
$$\frac{\partial^2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{sDA}}}{\partial \alpha^2} = \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha}\!\left[\sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}} \ell(f(x_i), y_i)\right].$$
Since the bracketed expression does not depend on $\alpha$ (all losses are constants for fixed $f$), its derivative with respect to $\alpha$ is zero:
$$\frac{\partial^2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{sDA}}}{\partial \alpha^2} = 0.$$

**S4 — Convexity/concavity classification (part b).**

By the second-derivative characterization stated in the world contract: a zero second derivative implies the function is affine in $\alpha$ — simultaneously convex and concave. Geometrically, the graph of $\mathcal{L}_{\text{sDA}}$ versus $\alpha$ (for fixed $f$) is a straight line with slope $\sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}} \ell(f(x_i), y_i)$ and zero curvature, so there is no interior minimum or maximum in $\alpha$ for fixed $f$; the optimal $\alpha$ is determined purely by the sign and magnitude of the target-child loss sum, not by any curvature of the objective landscape along the $\alpha$ axis.

最终答案：\boxed{\dfrac{\partial^2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{sDA}}}{\partial \alpha^2} = 0}

\textbf{Part (b):} Since the second derivative is identically zero, $\mathcal{L}_{\text{sDA}}$ is affine (simultaneously convex and concave) in $\alpha$ for any fixed classifier $f$; geometrically, the s-DA objective traces a straight line as $\alpha$ varies — increasing at the constant rate $\sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}} \ell(f(x_i), y_i)$ with no curvature — so there is no interior optimum in $\alpha$ for fixed $f$.
